As mentioned earlier, leaky relu tries to fix the dying relu problem. It uses the = function, where α is a very small number. In relu, when x ≤ 0, it returns 0, but in leaky relu, it will return the value. We generally keep the small value of α close to 0.01 or smaller.

 
Backpropagation
 
So far, we discussed how to update the parameters of the simple neural network, but we haven’t discussed how to compute the gradient of the cost function in a complex network. In other words, we have not discussed properly how to compute the gradient of the cost function with respect to each of the parameters of a network. So, in this section, we will discuss how each parameter affects the cost function and how to propagate the error back in the neural network to update model parameters.
 
In feedforward neural networks, we take an input x and then information from x flow through hidden layers to produce output . As information from x flows forward only, that’s why this process is known as forward propagation. Now, once we get the output, we define a J cost function, which represents the error between a true y output and predicted output. Using the backpropagation algorithm, we feed the information (that’s essentially the gradients) from the cost function back to the network. We can assume it as a process that uses the feedback mechanism to enhance its performance. In backpropagation, we feed information again to the network, but this time in backward direction. In other words, we propagate information in backward direction, that’s why this technique is known as “backpropagation”. Notice that even in the case of a generalized linear model, we carried out backpropagation. So, in general, we can say that backpropagation is used to compute the gradient of any function.
 
Moving forward, we will develop an intuitive understanding of backpropagation using the chain rule, which will be used recursively to compute the gradient of functions.

Overfitting and Underfitting
 
Now we understand what the feedforward neural network is, the different cost functions that are used to train the network along with different approaches to optimize those cost functions, and how the activation functions help in introducing no-linearity in neural network.
 
In any model learning, it is very important that the model is able to generalize from the training data to make predictions in the future on the data the model has never seen. But, in practical problems, either the model is able to learn too well from the training data that it even captures the noise and less important details, known as overfitting, or the model is not able to learn even the significant details i.e., it is neither able to fit the training data nor it is able to generalize for the unseen data, known as underfitting.
 
Ideally, with enough parameters, we can fit any data set. The fact that the model is agreeing well with the available training data set doesn’t make it a good one. The model should be able to generalize the scenario. In deep neural networks, we can have millions of parameters. So, it’s very easy for the model to overfit with those many free parameters (weights and biases). To train effectively, we should be able to detect when the model overfits.
 
It is not always easy to detect overfitting in a model. The general rule is when accuracy on the unforeseen data (test data) is low as compared to the training set accuracy, the model is overfitting the training data.
 
How to prevent overfitting in deep neural networks?
  
Obtaining more data
  
More the data, the easier it is for the model to capture all the significant details and estimate the parameters appropriately.
 
Train/Dev/Test set
  
In neural networks, there are a lot many hyperparameters to play with. Using the test set accuracy to set the hyperparameters leads to leaking of the test (unforeseen) data information, due to which the model fails miserably in production systems. Since in deep neural networks, we deal with millions of data points, it is always recommended to have a separate dev/validation set to fine tune the hyperparameters, keeping the test set completely unforeseen.
 
Reduce the size of the network
  
This approach is not used very often as larger networks have the potential to be more powerful than smaller networks.
 
Regularization: It is the most commonly used method for preventing overfitting. It basically adds an extra component (penalty term) to the cost function (Eg-4a) or modifies the network (Eg-4b), which punishes the model for being too complex and hence the model generalizes better. Different regularization techniques are explained below.
 
L1 and L2
  
Both L1 and L2 add an extra penalty term in the cost function so that network is able to learn smaller weights. In case, the penalty term is , and in the case of the penalty term is , where λ is the regularization hyperparameter. So, equation (22) becomes,,
 
  
Drop out
  
In this technique, neurons (or nodes) in each layer (except those belonging to the output layer) of the network are dropped out (deactivated) with probability which is a hyperparameter while training, with its default value usually set to 0.5. It is worth noting that all neurons are kept in activated state (no drop out) while testing/inferencing.
 
Early stopping
  
Many a times, it is observed that with the increase in epoch number, though training loss keeps on decreasing, validation accuracy stops increasing after a certain epoch. It is not necessary that the model received at the end of the training process is the best one that could be possibly created. Basically, we interrupt the training process before the model starts overfitting.
  
Although a less common problem with deep neural networks vis-a-vis overfitting, underfitting can also make the model inefficient by making the model overly simple and missing out on the significant details from the training data. Sometimes, keeping a very high regularization coefficient (λ) to avoid overfitting also ends up causing underfitting.
 
Underfitting is easier to detect with a good performance metric-like accuracy. The underfit model gives poor performance on testing as well as training data.
 
How to prevent underfitting in deep neural networks?
  
Add more number of layers or increase the number of neurons
  
With more number of layers or neurons, we try to create more free parameters for the model to estimate so that more details can be learned.
 
Decreasing the regularization coefficient
 
So far, we discussed nonlinear models and the nonlinear feedforward neural network. Now, we will see the difference between a generalized linear model and a neural network using examples. In this example, our aim is to visualize the decision boundary created by a linear and a nonlinear model.
 
Let’s start. First, we will generate a data set. For this, we will use a Python library called the scikit library, which has dataset generators.
 
#Begin of Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn import datasets
 
x, y = sklearn.datasets.make_moons(300, noise=0.30)
print len(x), len(y)
 
plt.scatter(x[:,0], x[:,1], s=40, c=y, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.show()
 
On executing the above lines of code, we will get a Figure as shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 2.22
 
#Begin Code
# Training the classifier
clf = sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegressionCV()
clf.fit(x, y)
 
# Train the logistic regression classifier
clf = sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegressionCV()
clf.fit(x, y)
 
# Set min and max values and give it some padding
x_min, x_max = x[:, 0].min() - .5, x[:, 0].max() + .5
y_min, y_max = x[:, 1].min() - .5, x[:, 1].max() + .5
# Generate a grid of points with distance h between them
h = 0.01
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, h), np.arange(y_min, y_max, h))
 
# Predict using classifier
Z = clf.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)
 
# Plot the contour and training examples
plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.scatter(x[:, 0], x[:, 1], c=y, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.title("Logistic Regression")
plt.show()

We will use x and y coordinates of each sample as an input. Now, in the hidden layer, we can set its dimension by choosing the number of hidden units, and these hidden units will define the complexity of the neural network. The more hidden units we will put, the more complex a function will be created. We can use any activation function, but in this example, we will use the tanh activation function. For optimization, the batch gradient descent technique has been used.

# Importing required packages
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
importsklearn.datasets
import matplotlib
 
# Generating dataset
np.random.seed(0)
x, y = sklearn.datasets.make_moons(300, noise=0.30)
plt.scatter(x[:,0], x[:,1], s=40, c=y, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
 
##defining variables
# number of training samples
num_examples = len(x)
 
# no. of units at input layer (input layer dimension)
nn_input_dim = 2
 
# no. of output units (output layer dimension)
nn_output_dim = 2
 
##hyperparameters
# learning rate used in gradient descent
alpha = 0.001
 
# regularization parameter
reg_lambda = 0.001
 
##evaluate the total loss on the dataset
#In this example, We are using tanh activation function, other functions can be applied to check the outcomes.
def calculate_loss(model):
loss = None
W1, b1, W2, b2 = model['W1'], model['b1'], model['W2'], model['b2']
# Forward propagation to calculate our predictions
z1 = x.dot(W1) + b1
a1 = np.tanh(z1)
z2 = a1.dot(W2) + b2
exp_scores = np.exp(z2)
probs = exp_scores / np.sum(exp_scores, axis=1, keepdims=True)#softmax loss
# Calculating the loss
corect_logprobs = -np.log(probs[range(num_examples), y])
data_loss = np.sum(corect_logprobs)/num_examples
# adding regularization parameter(L2 Regularization)to avoid overfitting
reg_loss = reg_lambda/2 * (np.sum(np.square(W1)) + np.sum(np.square(W2)))
loss = data_loss + reg_loss
return loss
 
# predict an output
def predict(model, x):
W1, b1, W2, b2 = model['W1'], model['b1'], model['W2'], model['b2']
# Forward propagation
z1 = x.dot(W1) + b1
a1 = np.tanh(z1)
z2 = a1.dot(W2) + b2
exp_scores = np.exp(z2)
probs = exp_scores / np.sum(exp_scores, axis=1, keepdims=True)
returnnp.argmax(probs, axis=1)
 
## Training neural network
# nn_hdim : no. of hidden unit in the hidden layer
#num_passes : no. of epochs
def build_model(nn_hdim, num_passes=40000, print_loss=False):
 
# Initialize the parameters to random values. We need to learn these.
np.random.seed(0)
W1 = np.random.randn(nn_input_dim, nn_hdim) / np.sqrt(nn_input_dim)
b1 = np.zeros((1, nn_hdim))
W2 = np.random.randn(nn_hdim, nn_output_dim) / np.sqrt(nn_hdim)
b2 = np.zeros((1, nn_output_dim))
 
# This is what we return at the end
model = {}
 
# Batch Gradient descent
for i in range(0, num_passes):
# Forward propagation
z1 = x.dot(W1) + b1
a1 = np.tanh(z1)
z2 = a1.dot(W2) + b2
exp_scores = np.exp(z2)
probs = exp_scores / np.sum(exp_scores, axis=1, keepdims=True)
# Backpropagation
delta3 = probs
delta3[range(num_examples), y] - = 1
dW2 = (a1.T).dot(delta3)
db2 = np.sum(delta3, axis=0, keepdims=True)
delta2 = delta3.dot(W2.T) * (1 - np.power(a1, 2))
dW1 = np.dot(x.T, delta2)
db1 = np.sum(delta2, axis=0)
# Adding regularization terms for weights, we can add regularization term for biases also
dW2 += reg_lambda * W2
dW1 += reg_lambda * W1
# Gradient descent parameter update
W1 += -alpha * dW1
b1 += -alpha * db1
W2 += -alpha * dW2
b2 += -alpha * db2
# Assign new parameters to the model
model = { 'W1': W1, 'b1': b1, 'W2': W2, 'b2': b2}
if print_loss and i % 1000 == 0:
print("Loss after iteration %i: %f" %(i, calculate_loss(model)))
return model
## Plot decision boundary
def plot_decision_boundary(pred_func):
# Set min and max values and give it some padding
x_min, x_max = x[:, 0].min() - .5, x[:, 0].max() + .5
y_min, y_max = x[:, 1].min() - .5, x[:, 1].max() + .5
h = 0.01
# Generate a grid of points with distance h between them
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, h), np.arange(y_min, y_max, h))
# Predict the function value for the whole gid
Z = pred_func(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)
# Plot the contour and training examples
plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.scatter(x[:, 0], x[:, 1], c=y, cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
# Build a model with a 3-dimensional hidden layer
model = build_model(3, print_loss=True)
# Plot the decision boundary
plot_decision_boundary(lambda x: predict(model, x))
plt.title("Decision Boundary for hidden layer size 3")
plt.show()

# Import required libraries
 
import numpy as np

Let’s assign various parameters and hyperparameters values of the network as follows:
 
# Units in first hidden layer
n_hidden_1 = 128
# Units in second hidden layer
n_hidden_2 = 128
# Fashion mnist data input (img shape: 28*28)
n_input = 784
# Fashion mnist total classes (0-9 digits), also, no. units in output layer
n_classes = 10
 
# Create placeholders
def create_placeholders(n_x, n_y):
#n_x and n_y represents size of input vector and no. of output class respectively.
X = tf.placeholder(tf.float32, [n_x, None], name="X")
Y = tf.placeholder(tf.float32, [n_y, None], name="Y")
return X, Y
 
def initialize_parameters():
#Initializes parameters to build a neural network with tensorflow. We have discussed
# earlier how to define shape of parameters at each layer.The shapes are:
 
W1 : [n_hidden_1, n_input]
b1 : [n_hidden_1, 1]
W2 : [n_hidden_2, n_hidden_1]
b2 : [n_hidden_2, 1]
W3 : [n_classes, n_hidden_2]
b3 : [n_classes, 1]
# Set random seed for reproducibility
tf.set_random_seed(42)
# Initialize weights and biases for each layer
W1 = tf.get_variable("W1", [n_hidden_1, n_input], initializer=tf.contrib.layers.xavier_initializer(seed=42))
b1 = tf.get_variable("b1", [n_hidden_1, 1], initializer=tf.zeros_initializer())
W2 = tf.get_variable("W2", [n_hidden_2, n_hidden_1], initializer=tf.contrib.layers.xavier_initializer(seed=42))
b2 = tf.get_variable("b2", [n_hidden_2, 1], initializer=tf.zeros_initializer())
W3 = tf.get_variable("W3", [n_classes, n_hidden_2], initializer=tf.contrib.layers.xavier_initializer(seed=42))
b3 = tf.get_variable("b3", [n_classes, 1], initializer=tf.zeros_initializer())
# Store initializations as a dictionary of parameters
parameters = {
"W1": W1,
"b1": b1,
"W2": W2,
"b2": b2,
"W3": W3,
"b3": b3
}
return parameters
}
 
def forward_propagation(X, parameters):
# X is the input placeholder, i.e. size of input and parameters are dictionary of parameters that
#we have defined in last function.
# Retrieve parameters from dictionary
W1 = parameters['W1']
b1 = parameters['b1']
W2 = parameters['W2']
b2 = parameters['b2']
W3 = parameters['W3']
b3 = parameters['b3']
#forward propagation, Z represents matrix multiplication and addition of bias value whereas
#as A represents implementation of activation function and integer associated with character
#represents layer no.
 
Z1 = tf.add(tf.matmul(W1,X), b1)
A1 = tf.nn.relu(Z1)
Z2 = tf.add(tf.matmul(W2,A1), b2)
A2 = tf.nn.relu(Z2)
Z3 = tf.add(tf.matmul(W3,A2), b3)
return Z3
def compute_cost(Z3, Y):
# compute loss between predicted output Z3 and final output Y. Softmax function is used # to compute loss.
 
logits = tf.transpose(Z3)
labels = tf.transpose(Y)
# Compute cost
cost = tf.reduce_mean(tf.nn.softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits=logits, labels=labels))
return cost
 
def model(train, test, learning_rate=0.0005, num_epochs=16, minibatch_size=32, print_cost=True, graph_filename='costs'):
# Ensure that model can be re run without overwriting tf variables
ops.reset_default_graph()
# For reproducibility
tf.set_random_seed(42)
 
# input and output shapes
(n_x, m) = train.images.T.shape
n_y = train.labels.T.shape[0]
costs = []
# Create placeholders of shape (n_x, n_y)
X, Y = create_placeholders(n_x, n_y)
 
# Initialize parameters
parameters = initialize_parameters()
# Forward propagation
Z3 = forward_propagation(X, parameters)
 
# Cost function
cost = compute_cost(Z3, Y)
# Backpropagation (using Adam optimizer)
optimizer = tf.train.AdamOptimizer(learning_rate).minimize(cost)
# Initialize variables
init = tf.global_variables_initializer()
# Start session to compute Tensorflow graph
withtf.Session() as sess:
# Run initialization
sess.run(init)
# Training loop
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
epoch_cost = 0.
num_minibatches = int(m / minibatch_size)
for i in range(num_minibatches):
# Get next batch of training data and labels
minibatch_X, minibatch_Y = train.next_batch(minibatch_size)
# Execute optimizer and cost function
_, minibatch_cost = sess.run([optimizer, cost], feed_dict={X: minibatch_X.T, Y: minibatch_Y.T})
# Update epoch cost
epoch_cost += minibatch_cost / num_minibatches
# Print the cost every epoch
if print_cost == True:
print("Cost after epoch {epoch_num}: {cost}".format(epoch_num=epoch, cost=epoch_cost))
costs.append(epoch_cost)
# Plot costs
plt.Figure(Figuresize=(16,5))
plt.plot(np.squeeze(costs), color='#2A688B')
plt.xlim(0, num_epochs-1)
plt.ylabel("cost")
plt.xlabel("iterations")
plt.title("learning rate = {rate}".format(rate=learning_rate))
plt.saveFigure(graph_filename, dpi=300)
plt.show()
# Save parameters
parameters = sess.run(parameters)
print("Parameters have been trained!")
# Calculate correct predictions
correct_prediction = tf.equal(tf.argmax(Z3), tf.argmax(Y))
# Calculate accuracy on test set
accuracy = tf.reduce_mean(tf.cast(correct_prediction, "float"))
print ("Train Accuracy:", accuracy.eval({X: train.images.T, Y: train.labels.T}))
print ("Test Accuracy:", accuracy.eval({X: test.images.T, Y: test.labels.T}))
return parameters
 
# Running model on Fashion mnist
train = fashion_mnist_dataset.train
test = fashion_mnist_dataset.test
parameters = model(train, test, learning_rate=0.0005, graph_filename='fashion_mnist_costs')

Conclusion
 
In this chapter, we discussed that linear models are useful against linearly separable data, but they fail against a data set with nonlinear interactions due to the inherent linearity, which means they can only identify linear decision boundary. In the real world, we generally encounter problems that cannot be solved using the linear decision boundary. Then, we discussed a nonlinear network called feedforward neural network. We saw how a nonlinear network solves the nonlinear data. Moving forward, we also talked about the various building blocks of the feedforward neural networks, such as cost functions (penalizing the wrong output), gradient descent (learning steps), activation functions (adding nonlinearity), and more. Next, we discussed how to avoid biases or variance in a network or how to make a generalized network. Finally, we concluded with a couple of examples—one showing the effects of complexity in a network, and the other on MNIST fashion clothes classification. A feedforward network is helpful to solve simple problems, but it does not show good results for complex tasks such as language translation, time series forecasting, object detection, and more. In the next chapter, we will discuss the extension of feedforward network, called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and we will see how CNNs help to overcome the limitation of feedforward networks.

CHAPTER 3
 
Convolutional Neural Networks
 
In the last chapter, we discussed feedforward neural networks, which are capable of learning higher dimensional, nonlinear, and complex functions for nonlinear mapping between input and output vectors. In this chapter, we will discuss a more advanced and complex class of neural networks called convolutional neural network (CNN). We will start with a discussion on the limitations of feedforward neural networks. Next, we will discuss the definition and applications of CNNs and how we can leverage CNNs to overcome the limitations of feedforward neural networks. Moving forward, we will discuss elementary operations and techniques required to build a CNN, such as convolution operation, pooling function, and more. Finally, we will conclude with the end-to-end architecture of CNN.

 
Structure
  
Convolution operation
 
Activation layer
 
Pooling layer
 
Dropout

 
Objectives
 
The goal of this chapter is to explain the applications of CNNs in processing topological data like images and to understand various state-of-the-art CNN architectures.

 
Introduction to CNN
 
Let’s start with the efficiency of the feedforward neural network. Generally, we come across data, like images and words having variables in the order of hundreds or thousands. To understand this, let’s consider a comparatively smaller neural network with 100 input units. Now, a fully connected first layer will have 10,000 weights and if we increase the number of layers to 3 or 4, this increases up to 30,000 to 40,000 weights. Even if we apply the general dropout criteria (discussed in the last chapter), it will not reduce the number of weights. Moreover, if we keep on dropping more hidden units, it will result in underfitting. That’s the case for a small neural network. Suppose, if we use a neural network with 1000 input units, the number of weights will be in millions. These many variables require large memory and eventually rule out the hardware implementation. Due to the conditions mentioned earlier, the implementation of feedforward neural network becomes computationally expensive. In addition to that, if we have limited training data, we may face the overfitting problem.
 
Apart from the computational limitations discussed above, there are also feature level limitations with feedforward neural network. We know that feedforward network is an unstructured network and does not share parameters and hence it is not robust to local distortions. During preprocessing, we normalize the data and feed into a network but there are chances of the image getting distorted translationally or rotationally during preprocessing, and since each unit uses different weights, the output of units get distorted. Secondly, in CNN, parameters get shared among inputs and hence the number of variables is reduced, and it becomes a much more efficient technique. Another limitation of neural network is, it does not use the topology of input data. We can see that we can feed input in any order and it will not change the output. But we know that images are spatially related, similar to time series that are temporally related. CNN exploits the correlation among local features. We will discuss later in detail, how CNN helps to overcome the limitations of feedforward neural networks.
 
CNN is widely practiced for data possessing grid-like topology. An example includes 1D data, like time series data that can be analyzed as a 1D grid sampled at regular time intervals, and multidimensional images, which can be visualized as 2D grid of pixels stacked in layers. CNN has shown remarkable performance in solving practical problems.
 
As the name suggests, CNN uses a mathematical operation called convolution without flipping the kernel. Mathematically, convolution is defined as a specialized kind of linear operation. If we analyze CNN, we can see that CNN is similar to neural networks that use convolution operation (cross-correlation) between weights and inputs in place of matrix multiplication in at least one of their layers.
 
Now, we will discuss what convolution is. Next, we will discuss figuratively, why researchers shifted their focus from fully connected network to convolutional neural networks.
 
As mentioned earlier, convolution operation used in CNN is not precisely the same as the one used in fields like engineering or mathematics. We will discuss several variants of the convolution operation that are widely practiced in neural networks. We will also see how we can use convolution function on various kinds of data with multiple dimensions.

 
Convolution operation
 
In general, convolution is an operation on two functions to produce the third function that is typically assumed as a modified version of one of the original functions. Let’s try to understand convolution with an example. Suppose, we are tracking the position of an object with radar sensor and our sensor provides the position of the object as an output, where is a function of time. Both variables x and t are real values; so, we may get a different reading from the sensor at any time instant. Let’s assume that the sensor produces noisy output. Due to noise in the output, we will get distorted results. To reduce the distortion, we will compute the mean of several measurements but we may not get an accurate result because we are giving equal weights to the variance of each measurement. To reduce the error, we use weighted average in which we give more weight to the recent terms. We can also think of it as a system in which data points are of varying quality, so the variance of random error will not be constant for all data and hence to reduce error, we can provide weights inversely proportional to the variance of data. To implement this technique, we can use a weight function say, w(a) where a denotes the time period. We can assume w as a probability function to get a weighted average otherwise output will not be a weighted average. Using this technique, we get a new smooth function which estimates the position of the object more accurately. Mathematically, we can write this as:
 
 
The operation mentioned above is known as the convolution operation. In literature, convolution operation is generally represented using an asterisk, * as = *
 
Let’s take another example to understand convolution operation. In this example, we will see more of a practical convolution problem, i.e. discrete convolution. Why CNN?
 
Figure 3.6 shows an example of an application of convolution. It shows how we can detect edges in an image using a type of kernel known as laplacian kernel. As shown in Figure functions and represent input image and kernel respectively, and function * represents convolution operation that produces filtered output.
 
 
Figure 3.6: Edge detection using convolution operation
 
Let’s understand the motivation behind CNN Figuratively in more detail. Assume a small image of size 3 × 3. In this example, the size of the image is restricted to 3 × 3 for simplicity and random numbers are used to represent the image.
 
 
Figure 3.7: 2D image (left) flattened into 1D vector (right)
 
In multilayer perceptron, input data should be so we have to convert data into vector as shown in Figure We can see that each pixel of the image is mapped to vector and we know that each element of the vector represents a single neuron in As we took an image of size 3 × 3, the total number of elements will be 9 and hence the input layer will have 9 neurons.
 
Now, we will have to decide the number of hidden layers. To keep it simple we will set 1 hidden layer and an output layer. Let’s take 16 neurons in hidden layer and, also, we are implementing a fully connected network so each neuron at input layer will be connected to each neuron in the hidden layer as shown in Figure In general terms, we can say that each neuron at layer l will be connected to all neurons at layer l-1.
 
 
Figure 3.8: Pixel from input layer is connected to each pixel in the next layer
 
In this example, there are 9 neurons in input layer and 16 neurons in hidden layer, so there will be 9 × 16 = 144 connections between neurons and hence there will be 144 weights corresponding to each connection, as shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 3.9: Fully connected layer
 
In this example, we have used a smaller image, so the number of parameters is small but what if we increase the size of an image? The number of parameters will be in millions for a large image. For example, if we use a image of size 64 × 64 × 3 with 2 hidden layers each having 1000 neurons or even 500 neurons, then the number of parameters will be more than 10 millions. Generally, for practical problems, image size is usually very large, and if we use fully connected MLP then the number of parameters will be more than 100 millions. As we discussed in the introduction, this many parameters will rule out the hardware implementations. CNN is used to overcome these types of problems.
 
We can see that the number of parameters get very large because, in fully connected network, all the neurons at layer l-1are connected to each neuron at layer l. To reduce the number of parameters, neurons at layer l-1can be connected to a group of neurons at layer l, as shown in Figure We can see that neuron with index 0 at input layer is connected to the first 4 neurons of the next layer with indices 0, 1, 2, 3, with the same weight as shown in Figure Whereas, in Figure it is shown that the same set of neurons is connected with different weights.
 
 
Figure 3.10: Each Pixel in input layer shares (same) weight with a group pixel in the next layer
 
So how many connections do we have now? Since each neuron is connected to a group of 4, the number of connections gets reduced to one-fourth. Hence, the total number of connections will be 144/4 = 36. We can see that the number of connections is reduced by 75%. Can it be reduced further? We will see that next.
 
In Figure the complete connection between each neuron at input layer to the next hidden layer is shown. For the sake of neat representation, a simple connection with one of the neurons from a group is shown here:
 
 
Figure 3.11: Fully connected layer where each pixel in input layer shares (same) weight with a group pixel in the next layer

 
Spatial relation among pixels
 
Till now we have seen that by grouping the neurons, the number of parameters can be decreased, but still the number of connections is not reduced. Is it necessary to connect each neuron with the neuron in the next layer? Let’s see. So far, we have not discussed spatial pixel relation in images. We know that in images, local pixels are highly correlated as compared to pixels that are far from each other. Is it necessary to use all the pixels of images at one neuron and repeat the same for other neurons also? This means, why are we connecting all neurons at layer l-1 to each neuron at layer l? Is it necessary or can we avoid this? Let’s understand with an example. In Figure a dog is shown with some background. We can see that and can also prove that the pixels representing the body are highly correlated as compared to the pixels between body and background.
 
 
Figure 3.12: An example image to explain spatial relation
 
Using all pixels makes the operation computationally redundant and expensive. Can we get the same result while connecting lesser pixels from input layer to each neuron in the hidden layer? We will get the affirmative result while discussing CNN further. Now, assuming that lesser pixels will give the same result, let’s see by how much the parameters can be reduced in our example. Okay, earlier we were connecting all 9 pixels from input layer to next layer; however, now we will use 4 local pixels. We can increase it to 9 or 25 for larger images but in our example, we have a maximum of 9 pixels and hence we’ve selected 4. Suppose, we are using the first pixel located at (0, 0) in the image and its neighbor pixels that are (0, 1), (1, 0) and (1, 1). As we know, local pixels are more correlated, that’s why 4 nearest pixels are selected. Now, each neuron at hidden layer will be connected by only 4 neurons from input layer. We have already formed the group of 4 pixels at hidden layer that share same weight parameters. So, in the above mentioned scenario, the total number of weight parameters will get reduced to 16 for the network shown in Figure If we compare this to the number of parameters for the fully connected network shown in Figure we find that the number of parameters is reduced by more than 88% for the network shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 3.13: Explaining spatial relation among pixels
 
We have discussed the limitations of feedforward neural networks. Now, we will discuss how CNN helps to overcome these issues. In the latter part of the above section, we have discussed how we can improve the efficiency of feedforward neural networks. In this section, we will discuss how CNN exploits similar features.

 
Convolution in 2D
 
In the above section, we have seen how sparse connections and parameters sharing between neurons reduce the number of parameters. Convolution provides the above mentioned features and apart from these it also exploits the equivariance features. We will discuss each of them in detail.
 
Let’s start with sparse connections. CNN make sparse connections using kernel. In feedforward network, we use an input matrix and matrix of neurons from the next layer to find the output matrix using matrix multiplication. We use full matrix from both layers and size of matrices is also high. What if we reduce the size of one of the matrices, i.e. what if we reduce the size of the kernel used in the processing of the image? Now, if we reduce the size of kernels in order of tens or hundreds, it will make connections sparse. Sparse connections mean fewer parameters, thus they reduce memory requirements and make computation efficient. We have seen for MLP how we can reduce the connections; for completeness, let’s see mathematically for the convolution also. Earlier we discussed for MLP, if input and output size is m and n respectively, then it requires at least m × n parameters and time complexity will be in × for each input. Stride
 
In this section, we will discuss how we can overcome the issue shown in Figure 3.18 using padding; we’ll also discuss the concept of stride. Firstly, we will start with “stride”. In Figure convolution between input matrix of size 5 × 5 and filter of size 3 × 3 is shown. In that example, filter convolves with input matrix by shifting 1 unit at a time. Stride is defined as the amount of shift filter takes after each step. For example, as shown in Figure filter shifts by 1 unit so stride is 1 but stride can be more than 1. In this book, kernel, filter, and feature detector will be used interchangeably. In many books, we often see the use of the word “receptive field”. It can be defined as the spatial extent of connectivity between kernel and input matrix at a time. As kernel shifts, receptive field shifts. So, if the size of a kernel is n×n then the size of a receptive field will also be n × Let’s look at the effect of stride with examples. Let’s imagine an input matrix of size 7 × 7 convolve with filter of size 3 × 3 with stride 1. This convolution produces an output matrix of size 5 × 5 as shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 3.25: Convolution with a stride of 1. Color box represents receptive field. Different color box represent receptive field at different positions.
 
Now, for the same input and kernel, let’s try stride of 2. Now, receptive field will shift by 2 units at a time. We can see in Figure 3.26 that it results in an output of size 3 × 3. We can say that as we increase the number of strides, the output size shrinks as well.
 
 
Figure 3.26: Convolution with stride of 2. Color box represents receptive field. Different color box represent receptive fields at different positions.
 
Now, what if we use stride of 3? In Figure it is shown that if we shift the kernel once more, then the space of the receptive will come out from the space of input matrix. In general, we select stride value such that the size of the output matrix remains integer not a fraction means full convolution not partial convolution.
 
 
Figure 3.27: Convolution with stride of 3. Color box represents receptive field. Different color box represent receptive field at different positions.

 
Padding
 
Normally, we increase the stride value if we want less overlap between receptive fields or to keep the spatial dimension small. But, what if we don’t want to shrink the size of the output matrix after every convolution step? Let’s understand how we can keep the size of an input and an output matrix same. We saw in Figure and 3.26 that after convolution layer, the size of the output matrix gets reduced. The output size is reduced because boundary pixels and non-boundary pixels are used differently. In other words, boundary pixels are used less than non-boundary pixels in receptive fields. Now, imagine if we build a deep convnet, what would be the size of the final output? As we build more layers, we will implement more convolutional layers and the output size will get reduced. So far, we know that the size of the output is reduced by convolutional layer but later on, we will discuss pooling layer which also reduces the size of the output matrix significantly. Reduction in the size results in the loss of input features meaning loss of information. In deep networks, we want to keep as much information about input features as possible so that we can extract low level features of input. As output shrinks, we find that the representation of input features becomes scarce which leads to high error prone results. Padding helps to overcome this problem. Let’s understand how padding helps. We will use the example shown in Figure The size of the input matrix is 5 × 5, kernel size is 3 × 3, and stride is 1. Our aim is to keep the output size same as input. We can understand “padding” more using Figure 3.28 and Figure Figure 3.28 shows the input matrix with zero padding (left) and the kernel (right) and Figure 3.29 shows the output of convolution operation between the padded input matrix and kernel:
 
 
Figure 3.28: Input matrix (left) and kernel (right). Color on borders represents different receptive fields.
 
 
Figure 3.29: Each color box represents output of a convolution operation between different receptive fields and input matrix.
 
We can see that the dimensions of the output matrix and the input matrix remained the same. We pad the input matrix with zeros. After padding, we can keep each pixel of the input image at the center of receptive fields during convolution. Hence, each pixel is used with equal frequency in receptive fields, which is not possible without padding except when the size of kernel is 1 × 1. When size of a kernel is 1 × 1, we don’t use padding because each pixel position acts as a receptive field, so each pixel is involved in receptive fields with equal frequency. We can pad additional layers with any number, like average of local pixels or maximum of local pixels but generally zero is used.
 
 
Figure 3.30: Example of convolution with padding and stride of 2
 
Figure 3.30 represents another example of convolution with padding and stride of 2. We can see that output matrix shrinks. In the last example, we used padding layer of size 1 and stride of 1 but in this example, we used padding layer of size 1 with stride of 2. So, how can we decide the combination of padding layer and stride to keep the dimensions of input and output same or how can we choose padding layers and stride so that we can get desired dimensions of the output?
 
Let’s start by simple convolution. When we convolve a 4 × 4 input matrix with 3 × 3 kernel, it produces a 2 × 2 output matrix. That’s because there are only 2 × 2 possible positions where 3 × 3 filter can fit into 4 × 4 input matrix. In general, if we convolve a matrix of size n × n with a kernel of size ⨍ × then the dimension of the output will be n – ⨍ + 1 × n – ⨍ + 1. When we introduce padding and stride, the equation changes. Let’s see the mathematical equation for different scenarios. Convolution in 3D image
 
Okay, so far we have discussed convolution for 2D data, such as 2D images. Let’s extend these concepts to 3D data, such as RGB (color) images. We know that 3D input consists of 3 layers where each layer is 2D, one stacked behind the other as shown in Figure To perform convolution with 3D input, kernel should also be 3D. In general, we can say that if an input is n dimensional, then to perform convolution, kernel should also be n dimensional. Let’s understand this with a 3D input consisting of 3 channels R, G, and B and kernel of depth 3. It means the size of the input is m × n × 3 and that of kernel is k × l × 3. We can see that the depth of both input and kernel is same. In general, we can write that if the size of an input is m × n × d then to perform the convolution, size of the kernel should be k × l × where, k and l are normally several orders magnitude smaller than m and n respectively.
 
 
Figure 3.38: Example of RGB layer of a 3D image
 
Why do we keep the depth of the input matrix and kernel same? In convolution, we perform element wise multiplication between input and kernel. In order to perform a convolutional operation with an N dimensional input, an N dimensional filter is required so that element wise operation can be performed at each layer. If we select the depth of a filter less than or greater than the depth of an input, it will result in dimensional mismatch error. It is a standard norm to convolve a layer of filter with a layer of the input image as shown in Figure To extract more features from the input image, we generally keep different values at each layer of the kernel. We can keep the same value at each layer or use the same layer as stack but then filters will produce scarce representation of input features and we know that scarcity leads to less information.
 
Now, convolution between input and filter will result 2D outputs corresponding to each layer as shown in Figure Blue squares represent layers of input, green squares represent different layers of a filter, purple squares represent results of the convolution operation between one layer of filter with the corresponding layer of input, and, finally, yellow squares represent stacked purple squares. To get the final 2D convolutional output, we add all the values at each layer along the depth to get an output as shown in Figure In our case, values in yellow squares will be summed up along its depth to produce single 2D input as shown in Figure In general, we use multiple kernels of the same size and depth to learn the input features. As mentioned earlier, each kernel produces a 2D output; hence, the use of multiple kernels produce multiple 2D outputs, one stacked behind another as shown in Figure 3.42 and This stacked output acts as an input for the next layer and so on. We will discuss the architecture using Figures in more detail.

Each layer of the output corresponds to a convolutional result of input and each of the filters. Now we are familiar with the terminology related to CNN and have also discussed the convolutional layer. Moving ahead, let’s discuss architecture of a CNN. Typically, a CNN architecture is composed of convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers. We have discussed the fully connected layer while discussing the feedforward network in the last chapter, and we have also discussed convolutional layer in earlier sections.

 
Pooling layer
 
Now, let’s understand the pooling layer. Pooling layer is somewhat similar to dropout layer in feedforward networks that was discussed in the last chapter. It helps to reduce the co-adaption between pixels and hence it reduces variance. In pooling layer, certain elements of the output are replaced with new elements based on the statistics of local output. Hence, it helps to down sample the data that eventually increases statistical efficiency and reduces memory requirements.
 
Right now, images are being used as examples, so we will use term pixels instead of elements and also because they are more familiar. For example, in average pooling, local pixels get replaced by average of those local pixels. Similarly, in max pooling, maximum value of pixel among local pixels replaces the remaining local pixels. There are other different types of pooling, such as weighted average pooling, norm pooling, or stochastic pooling, etc. Figure 3.46 represents two most commonly used variants, max pooling and average pooling. The left matrix in Figure 3.46 represents input image, the upper right matrix represents the output by applying max pool function, and the lower right matrix represents output of average pooling function. In this example, we can think that we are using filter of size 2 x 2 and stride = 2. These are the hyperparameters in pooling layers. Hyperparameters in the pooling layer remain fixed, meaning these parameters do not change during backpropagation, unlike weights and biases in convolutional layer which change during backpropagation.
 
 
Figure 3.46: Output after pooling function
 
The main function of pooling is to add invariance to small translation of the input which, essentially, means that a pooling function prevents the change in value of the output due to small translational perturbation in the input. We can understand the above statement using Figure
 
 
Figure 3.47: Representation of pooling function
 
In Figure diagrams a and b depict pooling function. In this Figure, stride of 1 and filter of size 1 x 3 has been used. In diagram the bottom circles represent outputs before pooling layer and the top row represents output of max pool function on the bottom row. Now, in diagram all the pixels shift by 1 unit; we can think of this as a small translational perturbation. Due to a shift in pixel by 1 unit, every value in the bottom circles has changed, whereas only half of the values of the upper circles have changed. This is because the max pool layer is sensitive to maximum value of pixels in the receptive field and not the pixel position.
 
We can also think of the pooling function as feature detectors. Suppose, we need to find a cat’s eye in an image; max pool layer ensures that if there is a cat’s eye in the image, it will detect it irrespective of its location but sometimes, we need to preserve the locations, and in that case pooling function will be inappropriate. For 3D inputs, we apply pooling function at each layer and then stack those layers.

 
Architecture of CNN
 
We have discussed the typical layers used in CNN architecture. Let’s understand CNN architecture with an example shown in Figure In this Figure, an RGB image of size 32 x 32 x 3 has been used. In the first convolutional layer, 6 filters of size 5 x 5 x 3 with stride 1 and no padding have been used and then ReLU function is used to induce nonlinearity. It produced an output of size 28 x 28 x 6; depth of the output is 6 because 6 filters of size 5 x 5 x 3 have been used. The next layer is a pooling layer in which a filter of size 2 x 2 with stride 2 is used for each output layer or we can assume that a filter of size 2 x 2 x 6 with stride 2 is used; both assumptions will result in the same output. Pooling layer downsampled the size by a factor of 2 and hence the output size is 14 x 14 x 6. Again, the next layer is a convolutional layer in which 16 filters of size 5 x 5 x 6 with ReLU, nonlinearity, stride 1, and no padding have been used, which resulted in an output of size 10 x 10 x 16. After this, a pooling layer is implemented with filter size of 2 and stride 2, which resulted in an output of size 5 x 5 x 16. Now, in the next layer, output from the second pooling layer is flattened into a 400 x 1 vector, i.e. 3D output is converted into a column vector. The next 2 layers are fully connected layers FC1 and FC2 with 120 and 84 units respectively, and finally, the softmax layer which classifies the input image. All the units from flattened column vector are densely connected to units of FC1; similarly, all the units of FC1 is connected to every unit of FC2. We can think of flattened vector as an input to MLP and then next layers as hidden layers of MLP.
 
Why do we add a fully connected layer? We can think like this—CNN helps to extract certain features from the image while the fully connected layer is (better) able to generalize from these features into the output-space. Fully connected layer helps to establish nonlinear relationship between features from CNN. We can also see that as the number of layers has increases, the size (height and width) of the image decreases but the number of channels (depth of image) increases.
 
 
Figure 3.48: A simple architecture of a CNN

 
Conclusion
 
In this chapter, we explored CNNs and the essential building blocks of a CNN architecture. Firstly, we have discussed the limitation of feedforward networks such as its computationally extensive process, inability to exploit spatial relations among pixels, etc., and how CNNs help to overcome those problems. We have looked at the important operations in CNNs, such as application of convolutional operation with kernel, selection of kernel size, concepts of stride and padding, max pool, and more. Moving forward, we discussed how to perform convolution operation at each layer. Towards the end, we learned to build a small CNN model. Once we are able to get small models working properly, we can build larger and deeper ones, following the same principles. In the next chapter, we will discuss various advanced and complex CNN architectures, such as Alexnet, VGG, Resnet, and more.

AlexNet
 
AlexNet, though a simple layout as compared to the modern architectures, created a deep interest in CNNs and their applications in computer vision problems. It was first designed by Alex Krizhevsky, Geoffrey Hinton, and IlyaSutskever from the University of Toronto in 2012 as part of the ImageNet challenge (yearly competition focused on image classification). It increased the ImageNet classification accuracy significantly in comparison to traditional methodologies.
 
AlexNet is composed of 5 convolutional layers followed by 3 fully connected layers as depicted in Figure Unlike the previously used standard activation functions, like Tanh or sigmoid, it uses the ReLu (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function, which helps in solving the vanishing gradient problem (discussed in Chapter Introduction to Neural Networks); hence it subsequently leads to faster training. To prevent overfitting and ensure generalization of the model, AlexNet uses drop out before the first and second fully connected layers.
 
 
Figure 4.2: AlexNet Architecture
 
https://www.learnopencv.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/AlexNet-1.png

 
VGG Net
 
VGG Net, first proposed by Visual Geometry Group, University of Oxford, is known for its simplicity using only 3 × 3 convolutional layers stacked on top of each other, unlike AlexNet which uses kernels of size 11 × 11 and 5 × 5 in the first two convolutional layers as shown in Figure
 
VGG Net is very appealing because of its uniform architecture and small filter sizes of 3 × 3 that help in reducing the total number of parameters. The blocks with the same filter size are applied multiple times. However, since VGG Net uses so many of such filters in different layers, the number of parameters is still large and sometimes becomes very difficult to handle due to heavy computation. The following image is about various depths:
 
 
Figure 4.3: VGG Nets of Various Depths

 
GoogLeNet/Inception network
 
After discussing and understanding the two important classic networks — AlexNet and VGGNet-16, let’s discuss the winner architecture of the ImageNet challenge 2014, GoogLeNet/Inception Network, which has proved to be an important milestone in the field of CNN architectures.
 
In the previous architectures that we discussed, the idea was to make the network deeper with an underlying hypothesis that deeper networks will always give better performance. But deeper networks have their own disadvantages, the first of them being the problem of vanishing gradients which makes the earlier layers of the network difficult to learn. With more number of layers, the number of trainable parameters (weights) also shoots up and training becomes computationally very expensive, both in terms of memory and time. Also, the deep networks are prone to overfitting; hence, they do not generalize well.
 
The network architecture of GoogLeNet builds upon the previous classical architectures and exploits some new techniques as discussed below, to deal with the aforementioned issues.
  
1 X 1 convolution
 
Though first introduced in the paper Network in Network as a technique to introduce non-linearity, 1 X 1 convolution has been used in GoogLeNet as a dimension reduction module that reduces the computation.
 
Let’s first understand what 1X1 convolution does in the following image:
 
 
Figure 4.4: 1 X 1 convolution for a 2D matrix
  
As shown in Figure for a 2D matrix, 1 X 1 convolution is simply a matrix multiplied with an integer and doesn’t make much sense. But when we consider it (images/matrices) with depth more than 1, as shown in Figure it helps in containing the depth of the layer or the number of feature maps in a layer. It is very useful because depth in convolutional layers increases with an increase in depth of the network and results in more parameters and hence more computations.
 
 
Figure 4.5: 1 X 1 convolution for a 3D matrix
 
Now, let’s try to understand how 1 X 1 helps in reducing the computation requirements with an example:
 
 
Figure 4.6: Without the use of 1 X 1 convolution
 
# of operations for convolution in Figure 4.6 = 14*14*48*5*5*480=112.9 M
 
 
Figure 4.7: With the use of 1 X 1 convolution
 
# of Operations for 1X1 in Figure 14*14*16*1*1*480= 1.5 M
 
# of Operations for 5X5 in Figure 4.7 = 14*14*48*5*5*16= 3.8 M
 
Total number of operations = 5.3M << 112.9M
 
It should be noted here that pooling layers (discussed in the last chapter) also reduce the number of parameters but the number of channels or feature maps remains unchanged.
  
Inception module
 
The idea behind using the inception module is to use convolutions of different sizes to capture information at varied scales. In Figure we see that convolutions of different sizes — 1 X 1, 3 X 3, and 5 X 5 have been used to extract all different levels of features from the previous layer. 1 X 1 convolutions in the yellow box in Figure serve the purpose of reducing the computations, as discussed in the previous section, by limiting the number of input channels.
 
 
Figure 4.8: Inception module
 
Global average pooling layer
 
In the architectures discussed above and in the previous chapter, fully connected layers are used at the end of the network as seen in Figure
 
 
Figure 4.9 Fully connected layer vs global average pooling
  
As can be observed from Figure in a fully connected case, all inputs are connected to each output, which results in 7 * 7 * 1024 * 1024 weights to be trained (total number of connections between the two layers).
 
Whereas, in the global average pooling case, each 7 X 7 slice gets mapped to 1 X 1 by average pooling all the 7 X 7 values, thereby creating a set of 1024 values with no parameters required to be estimated, unlike in the fully connected layer’s case. Thus, it saved a lot of computations. This simple trick of average pooling helped improve the top-1 accuracy by about 0.6%.

ResNets
 
Ideally, with an increase in the number of layers, model accuracy should improve. But, that doesn’t happen for all practical purposes, as earlier layers do not receive the required information for changing weights from network end due to increased depth — the vanishing gradient problem. Hence, training error starts increasing after a particular depth as shown in the graph in Figure 4.11 — often termed as degradation problem.
 
Introduced in 2015 by Microsoft Research as part of ImageNet Challenge 2015, and crossing all the previous benchmarks, residual Networks or ResNets have helped in solving the degradation problem to a great extent and gaining accuracy from training very deep neural networks.
 
 
Figure 4.11: Degradation problem in deep networks

 
Deep residual learning framework
 
Now, we understand that training a network better is not as straightforward as adding more layers to the network. We have a problem called the degradation of training accuracy. A deep residual learning framework has been proposed to address this problem.
 
As we can recall from previous chapters, every neural network, basically, tries to learn a mapping between input X and output Y with the help of stacked layers. In ResNets, however, instead of expecting layers to directly fit the underlying mapping we explicitly let the layers fit the residual mapping = –
 
Let’s understand what the intuition behind using residual mapping is, and how we achieve this through skip connections. From above, the unreferenced mapping function becomes = + where represents the stacked non-linear layers, and x represents the identity function (input=output). The idea is that it is easier to optimize residual mapping function than to optimize original unreferenced mapping function because mathematically, it is very easy to optimize = 0 than to optimize = x using a stack of non-linear CNN layers. This prevents neural networks from having to learn identity functions, if necessary.
 
To model the identity function, skip connections, as shown in Figure are used to explicitly copy weights from earlier layers to later layers.
 
 
Figure 4.12: Skip connections used for residual mapping
 
There are two kinds of residual skip connections:
  
When input and output are of the same dimensions, the identity connections are used directly as shown below:
 
 
When earlier and later layers have different dimensions, a linear projection is performed by the shortcut connections to match the dimensions as shown below:
 
  
Here, we should note that adds an extra set of parameters. To avoid that, we can also use zero padding for increasing dimensions.
 
Using these skip connections in a plain network, the final ResNet architecture is shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 4.13: Left: a plain network with 34 parameter layers. Right: a residual network with 34 parameter layers
 
In the last section, we discussed different CNN architectures that have been proposed in the last couple of years and have found their immense use in feature extraction for many computer vision applications. Because of all these advancements, it has been possible to train extremely deep neural networks and solve so many real-life image classification problems with great efficiency.
 
Computer vision applications and systems have become much more advanced and involved, and their use cases go far beyond than just image classification. Object detection and localization are two of them. Advancements in object detection and localization have made self-driving cars, video surveillance, face detection, robotic systems, and automation in many industrial applications, possible. The following image shows the difference between classification, localization, and object detection:
 
 
Figure 4.14: Difference between classification, localization, and object detection
 
In all such use cases, where we have more than one object in an image, and it is required to classify and label them after localizing, object detection and localization come into the picture.
 
Instead of just classifying the images into appropriate class, we need to detect all the different objects in the image and find their locations — create bounding boxes around objects. The last couple of years have witnessed the advent of many object detection algorithms, such as R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, SSD, and YOLO. In the next section, we will be discussing each of them and their architectures briefly, with a major focus on YOLOv3. This will be preceded by an overview of general object detection framework.
 
The steps in the General object detection framework are as follows:
  
First of all, the objective is to create and train an appropriate ConvNet (CNN) that classifies the different objects.
 
The next task is to find the regions of interest (RoI) or region proposals in the image through a model or an algorithm where objects to be detected are expected. Generally, selective search algorithm is used to find RoIs, which is a clustering-based approach that groups pixels and generate RoIs based on the generated clusters. These regions are represented with the help of bounding boxes encompassing the complete image. In the earlier object detection models, sliding window detector was used, and each window of a specific size from the original image was used instead of specific regions.
 
Next, we extract features from each of the bounding boxes, pass those features in the ConvNet created in step 1 for classification, and classify each of the bounding boxes into an appropriate class.
 
In the last step, overlapping bounding boxes are combined into a single bounding box, an approach known as non-maximum
 
The intuitive framework discussed above is R-CNN. Though it is very slow, it has inspired and helped the evolution of advanced object detection algorithms that we will be discussing further.

 
Fast R-CNN
 
Fast R-CNN is the immediate descendant of R-CNN. Although, it is quite similar to Fast R-CNN, it improved on its detection speed through two main augmentations, as discussed below.
  
Instead of first finding the RoIs and then extracting features from those bounding boxes, Fast R-CNN proposed to first extract features from the image and then use the appropriate feature RoIs for classification. Thus, running one CNN over the entire image instead of running 2k CNNs for 2k region proposals.
 
Instead of creating a separate model for classification, Fast R-CNN further extended the feature extraction model and included few fully connected layers and a softmax layer for end-to-end feature extraction and classification.

 
Faster R-CNN
 
Faster R-CNN proposed an alternative to selective search algorithm for finding region proposals in the form of a neural net. It introduced a Region Proposal Network (RPN) for this specific purpose. Now, let’s understand how RPN works.
 
After generating the feature map through CNN, a 3 X 3 sliding window is moved across the feature map, which maps the feature map into lower dimension. For each sliding window location, multiple possible regions are generated based on k default bounding boxes, known as anchor boxes. For each of these anchor boxes, we output an objectness score that tells whether or not the box contains an object and coordinates of the box.
 
Once we have these region proposals through RPN, they are fed straight into the Fast R-CNN, discussed earlier.

 
Single Shot Detector (SSD)
 
Single Shot Detector or SSD is a state-of-the-art real time object detection algorithm that provides enormous speed as compared to Faster R-CNN and also performs comparably well, but with a different approach.
 
So far, every model that we discussed had two components. First, we generate RoIs or region proposals and then we use ConvNets for classifying those regions. SSD does the two steps in a single shot. As it processes the image, it predicts both, the bounding box and the class.
 
Now, let’s understand how SSD achieves this once we have the input image and ground truth table for bounding boxes i.e. their coordinates and the objects they contain. Firstly, image is passed through a ConvNet (a series of convolutional layers) which generates sets of feature maps at different scales (to include different object size possibilities) – 10 X 10, 5 X 5, and 3 X 3. Now, for each location of different feature maps, 3 X 3 filter is used to evaluate a small set of default bounding boxes or anchor boxes. During training, ground truth box (GTB) is matched with the predicted box (PB) based on IoU (Intersection over Union metric). IoU is calculated as shown below:
 
IoU = (Common area shared by GTB and PB)/(Area of GTB + Area of PB-Common area shared by GTB and PB)
 
“The best predicted box is labeled as positive”, along with all other boxes that have an IoU with the truth > 0.5. Through this approach, a large number of bounding boxes are generated, as we classify and draw bounding boxes from every single position in the image, using multiple shapes, at several different scales. To overcome this, NMS or non-maximum suppression, discussed earlier, is used to combine highly overlapping boxes into one.
 
To summarize, SSD carries out region proposal and classification steps simultaneously. Given n classes, each bounding box is associated with 4+n dimensional vector that outputs 4 box offset coordinates and n class probabilities, and training is carried out by matching this vector with ground truth labels. Look at the following figure to understand the SSD framework:
 
 
Figure 4.15: SSD framework

 
You Only Look Once (YOLO)
 
You Only Look Once (YOLO) is another state-of-the-art real time object detection algorithm. Similar to SSD, it creates a unified network for predicting region proposals and object classes. Moreover, as the name suggests, even in YOLO, each image is processed once, but unlike SSD, YOLO does not generate the feature maps before evaluating the bounding boxes. Let’s get on to how YOLO actually works.
 
In the past couple of years, researchers have come up with different versions of YOLO, each one an inspired and improved version of the previous one — YOLOv1, YOLOv2, and YOLOv3 are the latest ones. We will primarily revolve our discussion around the latest version, YOLOv3, and the various ideas it has inherited from previous versions. From here onwards, YOLO should be read and understood as YOLOv3.
 
We discussed earlier that YOLO creates a unified network to achieve end-to-end training. Let’s understand this further. In YOLO, the input image is divided into an SXS grid as shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 4.16: YOLO unified detection
 
The grid cell, into which the center of a particular object falls, is responsible for detecting the object. Hence, each grid cell predicts B bounding boxes and the confidence score of those boxes that tell us if they contain an object. Bounding box is represented by where y are the coordinates of the center of the box relative to the bounds of grid cell, and h are the width and height relative to the whole image. During training, the objectness score (or confidence score) is predicted using logistic regression. It is 1 if the bounding box prior overlaps a ground truth object by more than any other bounding box prior. Only one bounding box prior is assigned for each ground truth object. Apart from bounding box, each grid cell also predicts the probability of each object of being a part of it. YOLOv2 and YOLOv3 do not use fully connected layers and rather use anchor boxes to predict bounding boxes similar to Faster R-CNN. One pooling layer is removed to increase the resolution of the output.
 
So, for one particular image scale, with 20 different objects, for a grid of 7 X 7, and keeping default bounding boxes as 2, YOLO output would look similar to Figure
 
 
Figure 4.17: YOLO output
 
Now, let’s discuss how we get the above output, and finally, predict the object location by training a convolutional neural network. Below, we have the DarkNet-53 architecture that YOLOv3 uses for predicting the bounding box and object class.
 
 
Figure 4.18: DarkNet-53 architecture
 
Note the presence of residual layers, discussed earlier in this chapter. Also, Batch Normalization is used in all the convolutional layers of YOLOv3 for better convergence and to avoid overfitting without using any other regularization approach. For class prediction, instead of using softmax, independent logistic classifiers are used for multi-label classification, and binary cross-entropy loss is used as there can be more than one label for an object, e.g. Woman and Person.
 
YOLOv3 runs significantly faster than the other detection methods, with comparable performance. Apart from the features discussed above, there are further improvements vis-a-vis the previous versions, such as direct location prediction, dimension-based clustering, feature upsampling, and concatenation. These improvements are responsible for its commendable performance. Let’s discuss each of them one by one.

 
Direct location prediction
 
While training, at early iterations, the model becomes very unstable as there are no constraints for bounding box prediction. Anchor box can end up at any point in the image. YOLOv3, (and YOLOv2 also!!) bounds the location using logistic activation σ, which makes the value fall between 0 to 1 (relative to the bounds of the grid cell). After constraining the location prediction, the parameterization is easier to learn, making the network more stable.
 
 
Figure 4.19: Bounding boxes with dimension priors and location prediction

 
Dimension cluster
 
While using anchor boxes for bounding box prediction, it is required to handpick the anchor boxes as has been the practice since the introduction of region proposal-based methods. In YOLOv3, instead of choosing priors by hand, clustering is run on the training set bounding boxes to automatically find good priors.
 
With standard with Euclidean distance, larger boxes generate more error than smaller boxes, but it is required to have priors with good IoU scores. So, the distance metric used for this purpose is:
 
 
Experimentally, it has been found that k = 5 is the best value with a good tradeoff between model complexity and high recall.

 
Feature upsampling and concatenation
 
YOLOv3 predicts boxes at 3 different scales to successfully capture small as well as large objects. Several convolutional layers are added to the base feature extractor Darknet-53. The last of these layers predicts the bounding box, objectness, and class predictions. Next, the feature map is taken from 2 previous layers and upsampled by 2×. This method allows us to get more meaningful semantic information from the upsampled features and finer-grained information from the earlier feature map. Then, a few more convolutional layers are added to process this combined feature map and eventually predict the output for each scale.
 
YOLOv3 performs better and faster than other technologies in the object detection world because of the design tricks that it applies, which we discussed above.

In this chapter, we covered a lot of state-of-the-art techniques and architectures. CHAPTER 5
 
Sequential Models
 
According to some, there’s nothing new beneath the sun. That seems dubious, but it is true that every seemingly new thing experienced is, in fact, the product of vast and unseen contexts. For example, humans don’t start to think from scratch every time new information appears. When, say, reading a book, understanding is built upon previous knowledge, either in a macro sense, such as understanding the language the words are written in or the tropes of gender, or in the micro sense, the context provided by earlier pages in the book being read. One name for these is sequential contexts. Even if thoughts seem novel, their novelty is born from a string of previous thoughts.

 
Structure
  
RNN
 
GRU
 
LSTM
 
Image captioning

 
Objective
 
After reading this chapter, we will learn how to get a semantic description of an image using deep recurrent networks and its interesting real-life applications.

 
RNN
 
Traditionally, whenever something was requested from a machine like a computer, it started anew each time. For example, when using a calculator, each new sum is a surprise to the machine; it has no memory of the previous mathematical habits of its users. This isn’t just a problem in simple machines like computers. There is a lack of sequential contexts in traditional neural networks, and this is a significant drawback, for example, when describing the kind of scenario that is happening at every point in a video or the subsequent scene in a video. How then to approach these types of problems? Traditional neural networks take all input at the same instant; hence, they don’t get any sequential data as an input. Due to the lack of structured input sequence, it becomes difficult to find the pattern in data and hence, impossible to predict what may come next, for example, prediction of a new frame using previous frames. It remains unclear for researchers to find how a traditional neural network can be used for sequential data.
 
Instead of trudging along with traditional neural networking, researchers shifted their focus and proposed a new algorithm called Recurrent Neural commonly known as RNN. An RNN is a class of artificial neural networks, which models data that has sequential property. As convolutional network is specialized for processing a grid of values such as an image, RNN is designed to recognize patterns in sequences of data, such as text, genomes, time series data from sensors, stock markets, and government agencies. It forms a directed graph, where a connection between two nodes can be across time instances.
 
If … are the data instances, where xi is the feature of the instance and yi is the corresponding label, then mathematically, an RNN model can be defined as:
 
 
where z is x2, …, xi − 1.
 
As evident from equation 5.1, RNN uses data from previous instances to return the output of data at current instances. Thus, RNN can be used for representing temporal or sequential information.
 
RNN uses loops in the network which helps to persist information.
 
 
Figure 5.1: Simple RNN with loops
 
Figure 5.1 represents a small building block of an RNN. As seen in the figure, it takes any input ‘xt’ and outputs a value ht. The above diagram also contains a loop; loops help to pass information in the network from one time-step to the next. For example, when reading a sentence, the first word is encountered, and then the second, the third and so on. Each word in a sentence represents a time-step. Comprehending the meaning of a sentence relies on following the entire sentence from the first word to the last and then understanding a relationship between them. Similarly, for machines, loops help to pass the information from previous time steps to the next time steps.
 
Figure 5.2 represents an unrolled diagram of an RNN in a chain like structure which shows that RNN can be used in sequence-like data.
 
 
Figure 5.2: An unrolled RNN
 
Now, each input, at different time instants can be shown. Each small block represented by A resembles a simple neuron. Hence, an RNN can be described as a collection of similar networks connected with each other at different time-steps, passing information to the next block.
 
In the last few years, RNNs have shown incredible improvements in the field of speech recognition, time series forecasting, image captioning, sequence classification, language translation, and many others.

 
Why RNN?
 
RNN exploits one of the early and important ideas of statistical learning, called parameter sharing across different parts of a model. Parameter sharing enables a model to generalize on the varying length of input sequence that is not seen during training. Let’s understand the importance of parameter sharing with these two sentences, It was raining in the morning and In the morning, it was raining. When we feed these two lines in a model and look for weather conditions in the morning, we expect raining as an answer, irrespective of the position of the word raining in both sentences.
 
Now, if we pass these sentences as inputs to a fully connected neural network, the network will have separate parameters for each of the sentences. So, a fully connected neural network needs to learn all the rules of a language separately at each position in the sentence, resulting in a large complex model with huge number of parameters. On the other hand, due to the parameter sharing property, RNN shares the same weights across several time steps, resulting in a less complex model and a lesser number of parameters. Also, a fully connected feedforward network maps only input to output vectors, whereas an RNN maps the entire history of previous inputs to each output.
 
We can understand the above statements more using Figure Suppose we have a sequential input in the form of Input1, Input2, and Input3, and our objective is to establish a relationship among these sequential inputs. Figure 5.3(a) depicts a feedforward network in which the input layer receives all the inputs at once and passes it to the next hidden layer followed by an activation layer, until it reaches the output layer. Each hidden layer has its own weights and biases; hence, each layer behaves independently.
 
 
Figure 5.3(a): Feedforward network
 
But our objective is to establish relationships among sequential inputs. How can we achieve that? To start with, we can provide inputs at hidden layers also, as shown in Figure But, still each hidden layer has its own weights and biases, and due to this, they behave independently and hence each hidden layer creates different rules for each of its input.
 
 
Figure 5.3(b): Inputs at hidden layers (with independent weights and biases)
 
To achieve our objective, apart from providing input at hidden layers, we should also use the same update rules at each hidden layer and, therefore, the same weights and biases, shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 5.3(c): Inputs at hidden layers (with same weights and biases)
 
Convolutional network also has the parameters sharing property (we apply the same kernel in a convolution operation), for example, convolution network can be used for sequential data, but due to the small size of kernel, parameter sharing is shallow. The output of convolution network is sequential, where each output unit is a function of a small number of its neighbor inputs.
 
In RNNs, each output unit is a function of all its previous units. Each output unit is produced using the same rule, and thus the parameters get shared through deep computational graph.

 
Forward pass
 
We can think of the forward pass of an RNN as similar to feedforward network with a single hidden layer, except that input to a hidden unit is from input layer and also from the previous timestep (output of previous timestep’s hidden unit).

Figure 5.4 depicts a more detailed view of an unrolled/unfolded view of a single layer of an RNN network. We think of each unit as a timestep. So, represents input to the network at time step For example, if we consider the sentence, It was raining in the morning, represents the first word It. Similarly, represents the second word was. Here, represents the hidden unit at each time step. As shown in Figure each hidden unit takes input at the current time step and also from the hidden unit at the previous time step.
