Variants of RNN
 
There are different types of RNNs depending on the architecture or depending on how the sequential information is captured. A broad overview of different types of RNN is mentioned below.
 
Let be the input vector, be the hidden unit vector, and be the output vector. and V are the weights at input layer, hidden layer, and output layer respectively; and are the bias parameters at hidden and output layer, and and are the activation functions at hidden and output layers respectively.
 
Vanilla RNN, also known as Elman has the temporal connection at the current hidden layer from the previous hidden layer at instant t – 1. In normal feedforward network, the hidden layer at t is only dependent on whereas, in the case of RNNs, there will be some component from instant t − 1 influencing the current output.
 
 
Jordan network is another variation of RNN where, the recurrent connection allows to use the information predicted at previous time step at the current time step. So a hidden layer at instant i.e. is dependent on the prediction at instant t – 1 i.e. –
 

 
Bidirectional RNNs
 
Alright, we have discussed common architectures of regular RNNs. Now, we will discuss another popular variant of RNNs called Bi-directional RNN. Before diving into its architecture and implementation, let’s understand the importance of Bi-direcitonal RNNs in practical problems such as text summarization or POS tagging.
 
A human brain reads the whole corpus of text before summarizing it. Reading the whole corpus makes easy for humans to derive latent intent and eventually helps to achieve better summarized results.
 
In general, a regular RNN model does not provide this feature to a machine. In regular RNNs, machine learns sequentially (word by word) from start to end. But like the human brain, it would be more beneficial to a machine when it could know the future words as well (learns from end to start). Bi-directional RNNs help a machine to achieve this feature.
 
Consider these two sequences of words “He said, Teddy bears are on sale” and “He said, Teddy Roosevelt was a great president”. Suppose our task is to tag names in each sentence. We can quickly identify that “Teddy” is the name of a person in the second sequence but not in the first because we can read the complete sentence and understand context from the latter part of the sentences. But, unidirectional RNNs do not provide this capability to a machine. Bi-directional RNNs help a machine to understand the context from the end. Figure 5.5 depicts architectural overview of Bi-directional RNN model.
 
 
Figure 5.5: Bi-directional RNN
 
Bidirectional RNNs are quite popular, especially in language translation and language modeling. As they capture dependency on the sequence from both directions so, the hidden layer output at instant is dependent on input from instant t – 1and instant t + 1. So, for bidirectional RNNs

Motivation for RNN
 
We have briefly discussed earlier how RNN can be useful. In this section, we will see more applications of RNNs. RNNs have shown great success in many natural language processing tasks. RNNs have been widely used in various domains which require sequential or temporal representation. A growing interest in RNNs has been lately observed in the computer vision community for video analytics. In this chapter, we will discuss how RNNs have been setting new benchmarks for video analytics. In the next section, we will discuss some applications of RNNs in natural language processing and video analytics domain. We will discuss the application in video analytics in great detail towards the end of this chapter.

 
Language modeling
 
Given a sequence of words, we want to predict the probability of each word according to the previous words. Let’s understand this with a simple example. Suppose, there is a need to fill in the blanks in the sentence the color of the sky is ____. A human brain can rapidly respond and say that the color of the sky is It can quickly offer blue as an answer because it knows the context of the question. A machine doesn’t have that context. In these types of questions, RNN can use previous contexts to find an appropriate word. These problems are classified under language modeling. An RNN based language model can generate word embedding, a latent space representation of the words. A language model allows us to predict the probability (likelihood) of grammatically and syntactically correct sentences by observing the sentences in the training dataset. As each sentence consists of m words, the probability of a sentence will be directly related to the product of probabilities of each word, given the occurrences of previous words. So, the probability of the sentence the color of the sky is blue would be the probability of blue given the color of the sky multiplied by the probability of is given the color of the sky and so on. Mathematically, this is:

Figure 5.6: Language modeling

 
Machine translation
 
Machine translation is an extension of language modeling in which two sequences of words are to be mapped. RNNs model the sequential information, where the input sequence from source language is mapped to an intermediate representation, which is then used to predict the output word in the target language. As shown in Figure the key difference is that the network will start producing output only if it sees all the inputs, because the first word of output (translated sentences) may require information captured from the complete input sequence.
 
 
Figure 5.7: Machine translation

 
Image Captioning
 
Together with convolutional neural networks, RNNs have been used as part of a model to generate descriptions for unlabeled images. It’s quite amazing how well this seems to work. The combined model even aligns the generated words with features found in the images. Since videos are a sequence of images, there has been a widespread application of RNN for video captioning. We will discuss the latest model in a later section. Figure 5.8a shows the example of image captioning. Figure 5.8(a) shows an image of a construction worker:

Figure 5.9: A simple architecture of Image captioning
 
CNNs excel at preserving spatial information and images, and RNNs work well with any kind of sequential data, such as generating a sequence of words. So by merging the two, we can get a model that can find patterns and images, and then use that information to help generate a description of those images.

 
Backward pass
 
Alright, so far, we have discussed the importance of RNNs and a few of its applications. Now, we will look into the learning process of an RNN network. While discussing the learning process in feedforward networks and CNNs, we have seen that given the partial derivatives of some differentiable loss function L with respect to the network outputs, the next step is to determine the derivatives with respect to the weights. We will extend the same concept to RNNs and will also discuss any additional concepts required in the learning process of RNNs. So, how are RNNs trained? Since now there is a temporal connection, in addition to normal feedforward connections, the weights associated with normal feedforward connections W can be learned using normal backpropagation algorithm. For the temporal weights backpropagation has to be slightly modified to incorporate the sequential factor. This algorithm is popularly known as backpropagation through time (BPTT).
 
Let’s consider a vanilla RNN network shown in Figure from equations 5.4 and 5.5, we can write hidden state and output at any time instant t as:
 
 
Here, we consider the cross-entropy loss between the correct label at time step and , the prediction of the network. The total error is just the sum of the errors at each time step, and we consider the average loss over the sample.

We will use the gradient descent techniques to calculate the weights of the matrices and We know that the total error at any iteration is the sum of the error at each output unit and, therefore, for any weight we can write that:

Vanishing gradient problem
 
As we discussed, RNN may be used to find the upcoming event using previous data, such as the description of the next frame using past frames in a video and the most suitable next words in a sentence. After knowing that RNNs are good for sequential data, can RNN be used to solve the real life complex problems? If yes, then how much previous data is required? How far any information can be passed to next blocks? Let’s understand this by revisiting the “fill in the blank” example. In that example, we had to find a more appropriate word to fill in the blanks in a sentence. Here is the same sentence, color of the sky is blue. We had discussed that in these types of questions, RNN can use previous context to find an appropriate word. Here, the difference between the relevant information and the word which needs to be predicted is small, shown in Figure hence RNN can find a suitable answer. But here is the catch; what if we increase the length of a sentence (means more words)? Can RNNs predict the word in that situation?
 
 
Figure 5.12: RNN with small information gap
 
Let’s take another example. Here is a sentence, I grew up in Spain; I speak fluent We need to predict the word after fluent. Let’s separate the sentence into two parts. First, I grew up in Spain and second, I speak fluent If we take the second part of the sentence as recent information, we can say that it suggests that the word after fluent will be a language. But it does not suggest which language. To know the type of language, we need a context from the first part of the sentence. Since, the number of words has been increased in this example, the gap between the relevant information and the point where the word needs to be predicted becomes large shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 5.13: RNN with large information gap
 
The increased gap results in more number of time steps and the value of gradient between output and inputs at initial time steps starts to diminish, which is defined as the Vanishing gradient. Vanishing gradient caused RNNs to have difficulties in learning long-range dependencies between words. To understand the vanishing gradient problem, let’s take a closer look at the gradient we calculated for W .
 
Let’s take another look at the gradient propagation through time, , which is a chain rule, along temporal path.
 
These gradients are stored in a matrix called Jacobian matrix, which contains all pairs of first order gradient propagation. If we apply the overall gradient update for any unit,
 
 
it turns out that the 2-norm (which we can think of as an absolute value) of the above Jacobian matrix has an upper bound of 1. This makes intuitive sense because tanh (sigmoid) activation function maps all values into a range between -1 and 1(0 to 1 for sigmoid), and the derivative is bounded by 1 (1/4 in the case of sigmoid) as well. For a detailed explanation of equation 22, please refer to this paper: On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks by RazvanPascanu, Tomas Mikolov, and YoshuaBengio.
 
Let’s look at the sigmoid and tanh activation functions. As you can see, that towards the limiting value, 0 and 1 in case of sigmoid and -1 and +1 in case of tanh, the function reaches saturation. So, the gradient in those regions is very small. As a result, the chain rule of gradient propagation, from layers that capture long range dependencies, exponentially reduces and finally vanishes. In other words, the that is the error propagation through time from the layer 3 to layer k through the temporal connection might vanish as k is large. This is popularly known as the vanishing gradient problem.
 
There is a related problem called exploding gradient. This happens on the portion of sigmoid or tanh curve where learning is very steep. As a result, the gradients are very large and if it happens in consecutive layers, the error propagation can exponentially increase and lead to an overflow of the variable storing the gradient. This is usually mitigated by capping the gradient over a certain value. It depends on the activation functions and network parameters; it can lead to exploding instead of vanishing gradients if the values of the Jacobian matrix are large.
 
There are a few ways to avoid the vanishing gradient problem.
  
Using proper activation function, i.e. using ReLU instead of sigmoid or tanh is effective in combating the vanishing and exploding gradient problem.
 
Initializing the network parameter using standard techniques.
 
Using other variants of RNNs, like LSTM or Grated Linear Units (GRUs).

 
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
 
How to solve the Vanishing gradient problem? The previous section actually contains the solution. To make the gradient propagate through a large context is not always required, especially near the training saturation. This means, when the network is near convergence, the activation function of the nodes is in the saturation region, where the gradient is small. In those instances, the gradient doesn’t need to be propagated through large context length. On the contrary, short-term context representation will mostly contribute to the error at that time. So, the network should have some control on what to remember and what to forget. In other words, the network should have some control based on the input and the hidden state which lets the gradient from previous state pass to the present state. LSTM does exactly that. Long Short-Term Memory, commonly known as LSTM, is another kind of RNN network, which can handle long-term dependencies between data. LSTM stemmed out as a saver for the vanishing and exploding gradient problem. LSTM has been used to solve many practical problems and has become a de facto standard for RNNs. The core idea behind LSTM is compared to RNN; it has several gates. This gate allows the LSTM cell to focus on or forget a specific part of the input sequence depending on the input and output.
 
LSTM becomes very popular by overcoming this problem and setting benchmarks in a number of fields in natural language processing, like language modeling, machine translation, image captioning, speech recognition, etc.
 
 
Figure 5.14: Simple structure of RNN
 
Figure 5.14 depicts an overview of the simple structure of RNN. It shows how information flows from the previous time step to the next step. In this figure, the box named tanh represents the tanh function. LSTMs also have similar chain like structures, but the small building block, which is called LSTM cell, has different structure as shown in Figure
 
 
Figure 5.15: Simple structure of LSTM
 
As evident from Figure there is a single neural network in a cell of RNN but in LSTM four different neural networks interacting with each other.

 
Architecture of LSTM
 
The trick of LSTM is the cell state, i.e. the upper line of LSTM cell, as shown in Figure It has a connection with some linear operations which makes it easy for information to pass along to the next cell.
 
 
Figure 5.16: Cell state
 
LSTM cells also have gates shown in Figure which decide the flow of information. The gate (known as forget gate) is composed of a sigmoid layer and pointwise multiplication operation.
 
 
Figure 5.17: Simple architecture of gate
 
Depending on the output from the sigmoid layer, it lets the information flow. The range of output values varies from 0 to 1. When the output value is 0, it does not allow information to flow, whereas, when the output value is 1, it allows all information to flow from last to the next cell.
 
As discussed above, the first step in the LSTM cell is to decide whether to pass the information from the last LSTM cell state to the next or not. The sigmoid layer, acting as forget gate layer, has already been discussed. There will be 2 inputs to the sigmoid layer. The first input, is input data to the network at time step t and is output from the last LSTM cell. These two values will concatenate together and act as one input for the sigmoid layer. Now, if the output from sigmoid layer is 1, then information from the last cell state, Ct – 1, will pass to the next cell. If the output is 0, then the information from the last cell state will not pass to the next cell. Figure 5.18 represents the forget gate with its respective equation.
 
Let’s go back to the example of trying to predict the next word based on all the previous words. In such a problem, the cell state might include the gender of the present subject, so that the correct pronouns can be used. When there is a new subject, the gender of the old subject needs to be forgotten.
 
 
Figure 5.18: Forget gate in LSTM cell
 
The next step is to decide what new information is to be stored in the cell state. This has two parts. First, a sigmoid layer called the input gate layer decides which values are to be updated. Next, a tanh layer creates a vector of new candidate values, that could be added to the state. In the next step, these two are combined to create an update to the state. In the example of the language model, their aim is to add the gender of the new subject to the cell state, to replace the old one that is to be forgotten.
 
 
Figure 5.19: Input gate in LSTM cell
 
In the next step, the old cell state, Ct – 1, will get updated into the new cell state The previous steps already decided what to do; it now needs to be done. From the previous cell state Ct – 1 and the new candidate cell state we generate the new cell state Ct by multiplying the old state by forgetting the things that were marked as ‘to be forgotten’ earlier. Next to be added is it Figure 5.20 shows the computation of new cell state This is the new candidate value, scaled by what the volume decided previously for each state value. This is a crucial development in LSTM over RNN. LSTM behaves like a memory cell, it not only stores the cell state directly, it learns what to store.
 
In the case of the language model, this is where the old subject’s gender could be dropped, and the new information could be added, as described in the previous steps.
 
 
Figure 5.20: Cell state computation in LSTM cell
 
Finally, the output needs to be decided, which is a filtered version of the cell state. First, a sigmoid layer is run, which decides what parts of the cell state are to be outputted. Then, the cell state is put through tanh (to push the values to be between −1 and 1) and multiplied by the output of the sigmoid gate. Now, only the desired elements are outputted.
 
For the language model example, since it only saw a subject, it might want to output information relevant to a verb, in case that’s what is coming next. For example, it might output whether the subject is singular or plural so that it is known what form a verb should be conjugated into if that’s what follows next.
 
 
Figure 5.21: Output gate in LSTM cell

 
Variants on LSTM
 
What we have discussed so far is a normal LSTM. But not all LSTMs are the same as the above. In fact, it seems like almost every paper involving LSTMs uses a slightly different version. Let’s see another form of LSTM briefly.
 
Gated Recurrent Unit, or GRU, combines the forget and input gates into a single update gate. It also merges the cell state and hidden state and makes some other changes. The resulting model is simpler than standard LSTM models and has been growing increasingly popular. Figure 5.22 shows a cell of GRU:
 
 
Figure 5.22: Gated Recurrent Unit
 
Peephole connection allows the forget and the input gate to access the cell state. Figure 5.23 shows a cell of peephole connection:

Application of RNNs in Image and Video Analytics
 
Automatically generating a description of an image, a problem known as image captioning, has recently received a lot of attention in Computer Vision. Image captioning is important for many reasons. For example, they can be used for Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) and therefore, it can be applied to many areas, including biomedicine, commerce, the military, education, digital libraries, web searching and many more. The descriptions can include where we are (e.g., street, playground), what we wear and importantly what we are doing there. Generating a meaningful natural language description of an image requires a level of image understanding that goes well beyond image classification and object detection. Mapping from the image space to the semantic space is the key challenge. Mapping the space between images and language, in our estimation, may resonate with some deeper vein of progress. Earlier, this was a difficult task; though images can be easily represented as Real vectors, there was no suitable way to capture the semantic and syntactic information of the text in a real vector. But with LSTM based language modeling, text can now be represented easily in a concise feature representation, which captures both the semantic and syntactic substrate. From such language models, each word can be mapped to a numeric vector representation.
 
CNNs have been widely used for image representation. The image classification model using CNNs have been widely studied, and it has been found that the intermediate output of the convolutional layers in such architecture is a feature representation of the image with superior discriminatory power, especially related to the supervisory signal that it has been exposed to.
 
The video caption generation or generating a textual summary for a video boils down to the task of generating the caption for individual frames or frames within the same temporal context. Since video frames are nothing but images, image captioning framework can start as a starting point for such a problem.
 
The fundamental idea is to map from the image space to text space. So, given an image the feature vector is extracted using a CNN, which is passed down to the RNN. Each I is associated with a sequence of words, i.e. caption, X = …., where T is the length of the caption sequence. So, the basic problem of caption generation is finding the probability of word sequence given
 
 
All the words are embedded in a fixed size embedding matrix of size . This word embedding matrix is learned by the RNN. Probability | is given by a where (hidden state) can be defined as:
 
 
where S is a nonlinear function.
 
 
Figure 5.24: Architecture for image captioning
 
As shown in Figure generally a pretrained convolutional neural network (may not be pretrained) extracts the features from our input image, then the feature vector is linearly transformed to match the input dimension of the LSTM network. Finally, the combined network is mimics as a language model with features vector as input.

 
Object recognition and captioning in video
 
In the field of computer vision, recognition and description of images and videos is a fundamental challenge. The object recognition task is more complicated in videos than in images, as different frames can refer to different objects, making detection more challenging. Ideally, a video model should allow processing of variable length input sequences, and also provide for variable length outputs, including generation of full length sentence descriptions that go beyond conventional one-versus-all prediction tasks. Networks that can play this role is called Long-Term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCNs), a class of architectures for visual recognition and description which combines convolutional layers and long-range temporal recursion. Figure 5.25 shows the architecture of LRCNs.
 
 
Figure 5.25: Long-Term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCNs)
 
In Figure 5.25 CNN (middle-left) extracts features from a variable-length visual input (left), those features are fed into a stack of LSTMs networks(middle-right), which finally produce a variable-length prediction (right). Both the CNN and LSTM weights are shared across time, resulting in a representation that scales to arbitrarily long sequences.
 
All frames with a length T sequence are input to one convolutional network. Therefore, ConvNet weights are applied for the entire time of the sequence. LRCN learns to predict the video activity class at every time step, and generates one label for the entire video clip by averaging each label probability.
 
 
Figure 5.26: Three variants of the LRCN image captioning architecture

 
Video description
 
In the video description the LSTM framework allows us to model the video as a variable length input stream. However, due to the limitations of available video description datasets, the LSTM input was generated using traditional activity and video processing methods, called Conditional Random Fields (CRF) activity recognition.
 
Figure 5.27 explores a joint object recognition and captioning framework using LSTM and CRF framework. For each architecture, we assume we have predictions of activity, tools, objects, and locations present in the video from a CRF based on the full video input. In this way, we observe the video as a whole at each time step, not incrementally frame by frame.
 
 
Figure 5.27: Video description
 
Each frame from the sampled pool of frames from the video and the CRF score for the objects are encoded by the LSTM. Basically, the Maximum Apriori Posteriori (MAP) estimates of the CRF is used to extract the video features.The LSTM decoder layer then tries to build the captioning from it.
 
In figure LSTM is used as a decoder and encoder, and CRF-max method is used to generate one-hot vector.
 
In figure LSTM is used as a decoder and full visual input representation is provided at each time step to the LSTM, like image captioning.
 
In figure again LSTM is used as a decoder but the probability is used as the input of LSTM not one-hot vector which helps LSTM to learn uncertainties.
 
For more detail, please refer to this paper: Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks for Visual Recognition and Description by Jeff Donahue et al.

 
Video classification
 
In today’s digital content video, in particular, has become a new way of communication between Internet users. Due to the pervasiveness of Internet, video data has been generated, published, and spread explosively. This has encouraged the development of advanced techniques for a broad range of video understanding applications including online advertising, video retrieval, video surveillance, etc. The sheer volume of video data has motivated approaches to automatically categorizing video content according to classes such as human activities and complex events.
 
We know that a video is a sequence of images. CNN algorithms are widely used in problems related to image and video processing. While discussing CNNs, we learned how CNN extracts latent features from images and how it can be useful. RNNs allow us to understand the context of a video frame, relative to the frames that came in sequence. Combination CNN - RNN architecture has shown good results in video classification problems. The video classification framework is a broad class of video analytics problem, which includes motion tracking, action recognition, and video type detection.
 
Video classification explores the application of LSTM beyond the prediction of short snippets related to video or video captioning. It explores the application of stacked CNN and LSTM for video classification. Given a set of videos V = … vn and label Yv = … the video classification problem tries to implement the CNN-LSTM stacked network to learn what type of frames distinguish one class from another. Here the LSTM, unlike the captioning problem, doesn’t learn the distribution over words; instead, it tries to learn the context of the video frame by frame. Alternatively, this is a problem of video understanding; as the previous CNN layer helps in image processing and feature generation.
 
Figure 5.28 depicts a two stream CNN-LSTM network for video classification. Specifically, the spatial and the short-term motion features are extracted separately by two Convolutional Neural Networks. The two streams have different functionality. One stream has the raw image as input. It captures the spatial features which is essential for object detection or recognizing the action in the video frames. Action detection is a difficult problem than object detection because, in action recognition, a lot of frames need to be summarized to form the action. This is where the second stream helps. The second stream has motion feature detection using Shift-CNN framework. The input are the shift features in the frame, and the CNN further tracks the object through the shift vector. Finally, LSTM networks are applied on top of the two features to further model longer-term temporal clues.
 
 
Figure 5.28: Video classification
 
Figure 5.28 depicts that for an input video, two types of features are extracted using the CNN from spatial frames and stacked motion optical flows respectively. The features are separately fed into two sets of LSTM networks for long term temporal modeling (Left and Right). In addition, we also employ a regularized feature fusion network to perform video-level feature fusion and classification (Middle). The outputs of the sequence-based LSTM and the video-level feature fusion network are combined to generate the final prediction.

 
Conclusion
 
In this chapter, we have explored the sequential models (RNNs/LSTMs). We have discussed why we need RNNs, its advantages over other algorithms, such as feedforward networks, and CNNs and its application. We have also looked into better versions of RNNs, such as GRU and LSTMs. In the end, we have also discussed how a combined architecture of CNN and RNN can be useful in problems related to images and videos. RNNs have been an active research area, it has shown remarkable results lately (most of all are using LSTMs).
